questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following values ​are possible outputs of  $f(x)={(1.5)}^{2x}-0.5?$ 

- $0$
- $-0.2$
- $-0.8$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite numeric cases; direct range comparison confirms stored key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "I and II only."
correct answer is "I and II only
Direct range comparison: f(x)>-1/2, so0 and-1/5 belong and-4/5 does not.
key_evidence.worked_solution:
The range of ${(1.5)}^{x}$ is

$$
{(1.5)}^{x}>0.
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches do not affect the range. Therefore,

$$
{(1.5)}^{2x}>0.
$$

Subtracting  $0.5$ from the above inequality yields the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{(1.5)}^{2x} & >0 \\ {(1.5)}^{2x}-0.5 & >0-0.5 \\ f(x) & >-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range is $f(x)>-0.5.$ Thus, of the given values, only $y=0$ and $y=-0.2$ are outputs of $y=f(x).$

We can also see that this is true from the graph of the function. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/58/5876d2095bfd91417d2e6395f8a02ae817ebd476076bae929d79709ea7961a3e.png)

So, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following augmented matrices have coefficient matrices in row echelon form? Treat the final column of each augmented matrix as its constants column.

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 11\end{aligned}],\,\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Stored solution explicitly tests coefficient matrix REF. Exact independent computation agrees with the stored key. Full augmented matrix REF gives a different subset, requiring an explicit coefficient-matrix question.

key_evidence.solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since ${a}_{32}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since the first row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & 11\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 6 & 8 \\ 0 & 3 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $C$ is in row echelon form.

A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}].

key_evidence.worked_solution:
A block lower triangular matrix can be partitioned so that it has only square blocks on the main diagonal, and the blocks above the main diagonal contain only zeros.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- $A$ is a block lower triangular matrix. Indeed, we can partition it as follows:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

- $B$ is a block lower triangular matrix. Indeed, we can partition it as follows:

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & 3 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

- $C$ is *not* a block lower triangular matrix since it can't be partitioned in the way described above:

$$
\begin{aligned}C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$A$ and $B$ only."

questions.proposed_prompt:
Let $⟨-4,y⟩$ be the solution of the system of equations below. 

$$
{\begin{aligned}9x+11y=-14 \\ 6x-ky=-34.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$
- **I.** $|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|=-4|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|$
- **II.** $|\begin{aligned}-14 & 1 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|=4|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|$
- **III.** $-4|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "I only"
correct answer is "I only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D} \\ -4 & =\frac{|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}|} \\ -4|\begin{aligned}9 & 11 \\ 6 & -k\end{aligned}| & =|\begin{aligned}-14 & 11 \\ -34 & -k\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is "I only".

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 7\end{aligned}],\,E=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: Therefore, only $Q$ and $E$ are elementary matrices.
key_evidence.worked_solution:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation. 

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $Q$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=3{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =Q\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $W$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

- The matrix $E$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from ${I}_{2}$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-4){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-4){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =E\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only $Q$ and $E$ are elementary matrices.

Let $⟨-1,y⟩$ be the solution of the system of equations below. 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}3x+5y=k \\ 2x-y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$

I. $|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|=-13$

II. $|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|=-1$

III. $|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|=13$

key_evidence.worked_solution:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-3-10 \\  & -13.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D} \\ -1 & =\frac{|\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}|}{-13} \\ |\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}| & =(-1)(-13) \\ |\begin{aligned}k & 5 \\ -4 & -1\end{aligned}| & =13\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is "III only".

key_evidence.worked_solution:
The intermediate value theorem can be applied on closed intervals on which the function is continuous. 

The function $f(x)=\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}$ is discontinuous at the values of $x$ which make the denominator $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ equal to zero. Therefore, $f(x)$ is discontinuous at $x=\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi $, where $n$ is any integer.

- On the interval $[0,1],$ we **can** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x.$

- On the interval $[1,2],$ we **cannot** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ because this interval contains the point of discontinuity $\frac{\pi }{2}≈1.57\,.$

- On the interval $[-1,0),$ we **cannot** apply the intermediate value theorem to $y=\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ because this interval is not closed.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Consider the following sentence:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{__________}\,.$*

Which of the following can be placed into the blank space to make a true statement?

I. $A$ has no inverse

II. $\text{rank}(A)=n$

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "I only."
correct answer is "I only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $A$ has no inverse.* $\,✓$  

Indeed,  a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)=n.$*$\,\times $

Since our matrix is not invertible, according to the invertible matrix theorem, it must be $\text{rank}(A)\ne n.$

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $det(A)=0,$ then all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.*  $\,\times $

Since $\text{rank}(A)\ne n$, it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))<n,$ which means that not all columns of $A$ are pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

- **I.** $g(x)=|x-1|$
- **II.** $f(x)={x}^{4}$
- **III.** $h(x)=\sqrt{x-1}$

solution_confirmation: Therefore, only function II satisfies the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,4].$
key_evidence.worked_solution:
For a function to satisfy the conditions of the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,4],$ the function must be continuous on $[0,4]$ and differentiable on $(0,4).$

Let's check each function individually.

- The function $g(x)=|x-1|$ is continuous on $[0,4]$ but has a corner at $x=1.$ Hence, it is not differentiable at $x=1,$ which means it is not differentiable on $(0,4).$ Therefore, $g(x)$ does not satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function $f(x)={x}^{4}$ is continuous and differentiable on $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ In particular, it is continuous on $[0,4]$ and differentiable on $(0,4).$ Therefore, $f(x)$ satisfies the conditions of the mean value theorem.

- The function  $h(x)=\sqrt{x-1}$ is not defined on $(-\infty ,1).$ Hence, it is not continuous on $[0,4].$ Therefore, $h(x)$ does not satisfiy the conditions of the mean value theorem.

Therefore, only function II satisfies the conditions for the mean value theorem over the interval $[0,4].$

- **I.** ${\sum }_{n=5}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{n}$
- **II.** ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }8{(2)}^{n}$
- **III.** ${\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{8}^{n+1}}{{16}^{n-1}}$

solution_confirmation: In conclusion, only series  I and III converge.
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Let's look at each series in turn.

- The series ${\sum }_{n=5}^{\infty }\frac{1}{2}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{n}$ starts with $n=5.$ So the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{6}}{{a}_{5}} & =\frac{\frac{1}{2}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{6}}{\frac{1}{2}{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{5}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

- The series ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }8{(2)}^{n}$ starts with $n=1.$ So the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{2}}{{a}_{1}} & =\frac{8{(2)}^{2}}{8{(2)}^{1}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is divergent because $|r|\ge 1.$

- The series ${\sum }_{n=0}^{\infty }\frac{{8}^{n+1}}{{16}^{n-1}}$ starts with $n=0.$ So the common ratio is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=\frac{{a}_{1}}{{a}_{0}} & =\frac{\frac{{8}^{1+1}}{{16}^{1-1}}}{\frac{{8}^{0+1}}{{16}^{0-1}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{8}^{2}}{{16}^{0}})}{(\frac{{8}^{1}}{{16}^{-1}})} \\  & =(\frac{{8}^{2}}{{16}^{0}})(\frac{{16}^{-1}}{{8}^{1}}) \\  & =(\frac{{8}^{2}}{1})(\frac{1}{16\cdot 8}) \\  & =\frac{8}{16} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the series is convergent because $|r|<1.$

In conclusion, only series  I and III converge.

Which of the following series converge?

I. ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!}$

II. ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}$

III. ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: In conclusion, only series I converges.
key_evidence.worked_solution:
We use the flowchart below to determine which tests to use for each series.

![](images/3a/3aa7f0243efeab51d00aa9694dd018245f7ca4664cc1a5fdf4e646aebb61536e.png)

With that in mind, let's test each series in turn.

- For the first series, we use the alternating series test. Observe that 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{1}{n!}
$$

is positive and decreasing for all $n\ge 1,$ and ${a}_{n}\to 0$ as $n\to \infty .$ So, by the alternating series test, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}{n!}
$$

is also convergent.

- For the second series, we use the limit comparison test. Let 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}\,{b}_{n}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

Working out the necessary limit, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n}}{{b}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}÷\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}\cdot \sqrt{n}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2n}{n+2}) \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{2}{(1+\frac{2}{n})}) \\  & =\frac{2}{1+0} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $L=2$ is positive and finite. Now, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}
$$

is divergent by the $p$-series test. So, the series 

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{2\sqrt{n}}{n+2}
$$

is also divergent by the limit comparison test.

- For the final series, we use the $n$th term test for divergence. Let 

$$
{a}_{n}=\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}
$$

Then, we have ${lim}_{n\to \infty }{a}_{n}=\infty ,$ since the polynomial in the numerator grows faster than the polynomial in the denominator. Therefore, by the $n$th term test, the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{n}^{3}}{n+2{n}^{2}}
$$

is divergent.

In conclusion, only series I converges.

Let $⟨-1,y⟩$ be the solution of the system of equations below. 

$$
{\begin{aligned}2x+ky=-4 \\ 3x-4y=5.\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$
- **I.** $|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|=-2|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|$
- **II.** $|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|=|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|$
- **III.** $|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|=-|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|$

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only"

key_evidence.worked_solution:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\frac{{D}_{x}}{D},$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}_{x} & =|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{{D}_{x}}{D} \\ -1 & =\frac{|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|}{|\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}|} \\ |\begin{aligned}2 & k \\ 3 & -4\end{aligned}| & =-|\begin{aligned}-4 & k \\ 5 & -4\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

So, the correct answer is "III only".

Therefore, the point $(1,\frac{\pi }{2})$ lies on the graph of $y=\operatorname{arcsin}⁡x.$

- Finally, we consider the point $(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{\pi }{6}).$ We note the following:

questions.worked_solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4}{{y}^{2}} & =c \\ 2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}-4 & =c{y}^{2} \\ 2{x}^{2}+(3-c){y}^{2} & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=3$ then the level curves are $x=\pm \sqrt{2},$ which consists of two vertical lines.

- If $c=0$ then the level curve is $2{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=4,$ which is an ellipse.

- If $c=1$ then the level curve is ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2,$ which is a circle.

So, only statements II and III are true.

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $[-1,1]$ is closed. The boundary points are $-1$, and $1.$ All of them lie in the set.

- $(3,5)\cup [2,3)$ has a boundary point $3$, which does not lie in the set.

- $(0,2]\cup (7,10]$ has a boundary point $0$, which does not lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following sets are open?
- **I.** $[-7,1]$
- **II.** $(-1,3]\cup [4,5)$
- **III.** $(-5,-1)$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only"
correct answer is "III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Recall that:

- A set is *open* if it does not contain any of its boundary points. In other words, an open set consists only of the interior points of the set.

- A set is *closed* if it contains **all** of its boundary points. In other words, a closed set consists of all the interior and all the boundary points of the set.

Among the given sets, only $(-5,-1)$ is open. The boundary points are $-5$, and $-1.$ None of them lie in the set.

The other sets are not open because:

- $[-7,1]$ has two boundary points $-7$, and $1$, and both of them lie in the set.

- $(-1,3]\cup [4,5)$ has four boundary points $-1$, $3$, $4$, and $5$, and the points $3$ and $4$ lie in the set.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following equalities are true given that
$D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,\frac{1}{2}\le y\le 1}.$
- **I.** ${∬}_{D}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}A={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y$
- **II.** ${∬}_{D}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}A={\int }_{1/2}^{1}{\int }_{1}^{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$
- **III.** ${∬}_{D}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}A={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1/2}^{1}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only"
correct answer is "III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
We notice that:

- the limits for the variable $x$ are from $1$ to $2$, and

- the limits for the variable $y$ are from $\frac{1}{2}$ to $1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1/2}^{1}[{\int }_{1}^{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the region of integration is rectangular, we can simply swap the order of integration. This gives

$$
{∬}_{D}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}A={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{1/2}^{1}y\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x.
$$

So, the correct answer is "III only".

- **III.** It's neither a type I nor a type II region
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\, & ⟹\,x=\pm \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}} \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1\, & ⟹\,y=\pm \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's sketch our region.

![](images/09/0960063edcce8ccd55dc2f77147c4a4982645c180e8b998d7e520c65131ea045.png)

We have the following:

- Any vertical line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\le y\le \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}\}.
$$

So, this is a type I region.

- Any horizontal line through the region intersects it on a single interval. Furthermore, we can represent our region as

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,-\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\le x\le \sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}\}.
$$

So, this is a type II region.

Therefore, only statements I and II are true.

A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

solution_confirmation: Therefore, only $B$ and $C$ are **not** in row echelon form.
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Remember that a matrix is in row echelon form if it satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The matrix $A$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 3 & 4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since the leading entry ${c}_{32}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated). 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 0 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, only $B$ and $C$ are **not** in row echelon form.

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the bottom of the matrix.
- Each leading entry of a row is in a column to the right of the leading entry of the row above it.

- The matrix $A$ is not in row echelon form since the second row contains only zeros and it is not at the bottom of the matrix (condition I is violated).

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $B$ is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not in row echelon form since ${c}_{21}\ne 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 5 & 8 \\ 1 & -4 & 0 & 6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

- The set $A$ is not a subspace because it does not contain the zero vector. Indeed, $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ does not satisfy the equation $1-x-y=0$ since $1-0-0\ne 0.$

- The set $C$ is a subspace. It represents a plane, and a plane is a subspace if and only if it passes through the origin. Here, the components of the zero vector $0=⟨0,0,0⟩$ satisfy the equation $2x+3y-z=0$ since $2\cdot 0+3\cdot 0-0=0.$ So $0$ lies in $C.$

Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}
$$

I. The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$

II. The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$

III. The limit exists and is equal to $2$

atomic_options.label: II
atomic_options.text: The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
atomic_options.proof: Along y=x^2, the ratio is 2x^2/x^2=2 for x!=0.

$$

$$

questions.problem_after:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the limit given below?

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}
$$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $y=x$
- **II.** The limit evaluates to $2$ along the path $y={x}^{2}$
- **III.** The limit exists and is equal to $2$
questions.worked_solution:
Attempting to evaluate the limit by direct substitution leads to the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}:$

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\frac{2\cdot {0}^{2}}{2\cdot {0}^{2}-0}=\frac{0}{0}
$$

However, the function cannot be simplified by canceling common factors in the numerator and denominator:

We attempt to evaluate the limit by approaching $(0,0)$ from different paths.

- Statement I is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y=x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y=x}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{x(2x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{2x-1} \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 0}{2\cdot 0-1} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is also true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $y={x}^{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{2}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}}{2{x}^{2}-y}=\text{DNE}
$$

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following products is the LU factorization of a matrix $C?$
- **I.** $C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]$
- **II.** $C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]$
- **III.** $C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only"
correct answer is "III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Remember that in the LU factorization of a matrix $C,$ we write $C=LU$ where the matrix $L$ is a unit lower triangular matrix (a lower triangular matrix that has only $1$'s on the main diagonal) and the matrix $U$ is an upper triangular matrix:

$$
C=\overset{L}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ ∗ & 1\end{aligned}]}}\cdot \overset{U}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & ∗\end{aligned}]}}
$$

With that in mind, let's inspect each product in turn.

- The first product is *not* in $LU$ form  because  the matrix on the left is not a unit lower triangular matrix, as its main diagonal contains a number not equal to $1.$

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\,\times 
$$

- The second product is *not* in $LU$ form. Although we have a product of an upper triangular matrix on the left and a unit lower triangular matrix on the right, the order of multiplication is not correct (instead, we need a unit lower triangular matrix on the left and an upper triangular matrix on the right).

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,\times 
$$

- The third product is in $LU$ form because the left matrix is a unit lower triangular matrix, and the right matrix is an upper triangular matrix. 

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]\,✓
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only".

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Remember that the eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ With that in mind, let's examine the statements one by one.

- Statement is false. By the definition of an eigenvector, we have 

$$
Av=2v.
$$

 
Multiplying it by ${A}^{-1}$ from the left, we obtain 

$$
v=2{A}^{-1}v.
$$

Dividing both sides by $2$, we get 

$$
{A}^{-1}v=\frac{1}{2}v.
$$

 
So, $v$ is an eigenvector  of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{2}.$

**Note:** In general, an eigenvector of an invertible matrix $A$ that corresponds to an eigenvalue $\lambda $ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\frac{1}{\lambda }.$

- Statement II is true. According to the statement above, an eigenvector of $A$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ is an eigenvector of ${A}^{-1}$ that corresponds to $\lambda =\frac{1}{1}=1.$

- Statement III is false. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}A(7v)=7Av=7(2v)=2(7v).\end{aligned}
$$

Since, $A(7v)=2(7v),$ and $7v\ne 0,$ this implies that $7v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ and the corresponding eigenvalue is $\lambda =2.$

**Note:** In general, any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is again an eigenvector, and the corresponding eigenvalue is the same.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
The invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=n=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the options separately.

- The following statement is false:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $A$ is **not** invertible.* $\,\times $

By the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ we must have that $A$ is invertible.

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{rank}(A)=n.$* $\,✓$ 

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{rank}(A)=\text{dim(Col}(A))=n.$

- The following statement is true:

*If $A$ is a $n\times n$ matrix and $\text{nullity}(A)=0,$ then $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}.$* $\,✓$

Indeed, since $A$ is invertible, then according to the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{n}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

The general solution is the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution:

$$
y(t)={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t)

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2}+16 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}]=kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}], \\  & T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}]=T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}kx \\ ky\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}kx+ky \\ 2(ky)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}k(x+y) \\ k(2y)\end{aligned}] \\  & =k[\begin{aligned}x+y \\ 2y\end{aligned}] \\  & =kT[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{y}_{1}+{y}_{2} \\ 2({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{y}_{1} \\ 2{y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+{y}_{2} \\ 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{aligned}]+T[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is a linear transformation.

As a result, all three statements are true.

- $N$ represents the set of **natural numbers**.

$$
-\frac{27}{3}\notin N.

$$
-\frac{27}{3}\in Z.
$$

- Every integer is a rational, real, and complex number. Consequently, $-\frac{27}{3}$ belongs to $Q,R,$ and $C,$ and we can write

$$
-\frac{27}{3}\in Q,\,-\frac{27}{3}\in R,\,-\frac{27}{3}\in C.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$Z,Q,R,$ and $C$ only."

Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$
- **I.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=2x{y}^{2}-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-2x$
- **II.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=yx{e}^{x}+{y}^{2}$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=(x-1){e}^{x}+2xy$
- **III.** ${f}_{x}(x,y)=x-y$ and ${f}_{y}(x,y)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-x$

Select all that apply.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is 'II and III only'
correct answer is 'II and III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

- For the first pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x{y}^{2}-y)=4xy-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2{x}^{2}y-2x)=4xy-2.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)\ne {f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the second pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(yx{e}^{x}+{y}^{2})=x{e}^{x}+2y \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x-1){e}^{x}+2xy)=x{e}^{x}+2y.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

- For the third pair, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-y)=-1 \\ {f}_{yx}(x,y) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡y}-x)=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

As ${f}_{xy}(x,y)={f}_{yx}(x,y)$,  the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2},{u}_{3}\},$ 
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\},$ respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- $\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0 \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{3}=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot {u}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- $\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0 \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{3}=0 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1 \\ {w}_{3}\cdot {w}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -5 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=1+25+4=30\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $U$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $V,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{6}{13}+\frac{6}{13}=0 & ✓ \\ {v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}=1 & ✓ \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{13}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $V$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $W,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{18}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}=0 & ✓ \\ {w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{6}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{4}{6}+\frac{1}{6}=1 & ✓ \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{3}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $W$ is orthonormal.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$V$ and $W$ only".

key_evidence.worked_solution:
A rotation-scaling matrix has the form 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & -b \\ b & a\end{aligned}],
$$

 where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers that are not equal to zero simultaneously. Notice that the entries on the main diagonal are the same, while the antidiagonal entries have opposite signs.

With that in mind let's check each of the given matrices:

- $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]$ is *not* a rotation-scaling matrix since the entries on the antidiagonal do not have opposite signs.

- $B=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}]$ is a rotation-scaling matrix.

- $C=[\begin{aligned}8 & 4 \\ -4 & -8\end{aligned}]$ is *not* a rotation-scaling matrix since the entries on the main diagonal are not the same.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "II only."

$$

$$

key_evidence.worked_solution:
A random variable is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment.

A *discrete* random variable is a random variable

- that has finitely many possible values, or

- whose possible values can be listed in a sequence: ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},…$

Remember that a real interval (e.g. $(a,b)$ or $[a,b]$) cannot be listed in a sequence.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I does *not* describe a discrete random variable. The number of hearts in a particular complete deck of cards is not the outcome of a trial or experiment.

- Statement II describes a discrete random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and its possible values can be listed in a sequence: $0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7.$

- Statement III describes a discrete random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and we can count its possible values in a sequence: $1,2,3,…$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to zero due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{cos}⁡((-x)^{2}) \\  & =-x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2}) \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}x\operatorname{cos}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+1)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x+1) \\  & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡(1-x) \\  & \ne -g(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $h(x)={x}^{3}-2x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =(-x)^{3}-2(-x) \\  & =-{x}^{3}+2x \\  & =-({x}^{3}-2x) \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }({x}^{3}-2x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?
- **I.** ${\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x$
- **II.** ${\int }_{-2}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x$
- **III.** ${\int }_{-1}^{1}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x$

Select all that apply.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3(-x)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ is an odd function, but integral II is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}g(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

- The function $h(x)=2\operatorname{tan}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}h(-x) & =2\operatorname{tan}⁡(-x) \\  & =-2\operatorname{tan}⁡x \\  & =-h(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\operatorname{tan}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "III only."

questions.proposed_prompt:
Which of the following are discrete random variables?
- **I.** The exact time (not rounded to integers) that a full charge of a phone battery lasts
- **II.** The number of pets owned by a randomly selected family in a town
- **III.** The height of a randomly selected plant in a nursery

Select all that apply.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "II only."
correct answer is "II only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
A random variable is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment.

A *discrete* random variable is a random variable

- that has finitely many possible values, or

- whose possible values can be listed in a sequence: ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3},…$

Remember that a real interval (e.g. $(a,b)$ or $[a,b]$) cannot be listed in a sequence.

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I does not describe a discrete random variable. Although its value is determined by the result of an experiment, the possible values are real numbers that cannot be listed in a sequence.

- Statement II describes a discrete random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and it has finitely many possible values: $0,1,2,3,….$

- Statement III does not describe a discrete random variable. Although its value is determined by the result of an experiment, the possible values are real numbers that cannot be listed in a sequence.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.proposed_prompt:
Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The triangle $S$ is mapped to the triangle ${S}^{′}$ under the action of $T.$ The triangle ${S}^{′}$ has vertices $(3,2),(14,6),$ and $(9,2).$ Which of the following are vertices of $S?$
- **I.** $(3,2)$
- **II.** $(1,1)$
- **III.** $(5,1)$

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only."
correct answer is "III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
First, we create a matrix $Y$ containing all of the vertices of ${S}^{′}:$ 

$$
Y=[\begin{aligned}3 & 14 & 9 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, if $X$ denotes the matrix that contains the corresponding vertices of $S$, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot X & =Y \\ T\cdot X & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 14 & 9 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We need to reverse the action of the matrix $T.$ So, we multiply the above equation by ${T}^{-1},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}\cdot T\cdot X & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 14 & 9 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] \\ X & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 14 & 9 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse of $T$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2-0}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}X & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 14 & 9 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 14 & 9 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 & 10 \\ 2 & 6 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 5 \\ 1 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, the coordinates of the vertices of the original triangle are $(-1,1),(2,3),(5,1).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Y=[\begin{aligned}4 & 17 & 10 \\ -1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T\cdot X & =Y \\ T\cdot X & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 17 & 10 \\ -1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}\cdot T\cdot X & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 17 & 10 \\ -1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\ X & ={T}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 17 & 10 \\ -1 & -3 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{-1-0}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -5 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$

questions.proposed_prompt:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The position of the particle $y(t)$ at time $t$ is governed by the equation

$$
{y}^{″}+16y=32t.
$$

Which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t+ϕ)+16t$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡2t+8t$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R$ and $ϕ$ are constants.

Select all that apply.
questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "II only"
correct answer is "II only
Only II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".
key_evidence.worked_solution:
The general solution is the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution:

$$
y(t)={y}_{c}(t)+{y}_{p}(t)
$$

First, we find the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(t),$ which is the solution to the simple harmonic motion equation ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=0.$ It can be written in three different forms:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t$

In our case

$$
{\omega }^{2}=16\,⟹\,\omega =4.
$$

Thus, we have:

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

- ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t$

Next, we find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(t).$ Since the external force is a linear function, we assume that the particular solution is also a linear function,

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\alpha t+\beta .
$$

By substituting the particular solution into the differential equation and equating coefficients, we find that $\alpha =2$ and $\beta =0.$ So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=2t.
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t, \\ y(t) & =R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+2t, \\ y(t) & =A\operatorname{cos}⁡4t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡4t+2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Only II matches the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

Consider the vector $x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ By evaluating the following quadratic forms at $x$ **only,** determine which of them **cannot** be negative-definite.
- **I.** $R(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}$
- **II.** $S(x)={x}^{T}\,[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]x$
- **III.** $T(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}$

Select all that apply.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "II and III only."
correct answer is "II and III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
A quadratic form $Q(x)$ is negative-definite if $Q(x)<0$ for all $x\in {R}^{n}∖{0}.$

With that in mind, let's examine each of the quadratic forms by substituting $x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]:$

- Quadratic form I *might* be negative-definite. Indeed, 

$$
\begin{aligned}R(x) & =(-1)^{2}-{3}^{2} \\  & =1-9 \\  & =-8<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form II *cannot* be negative-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =33>0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Quadratic form III *cannot* be negative-definite since

$$
\begin{aligned}T(x) & =(-1)^{2}+3(3)^{2} \\  & =1+27 \\  & =28>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

Which of the following quadratic forms over ${R}^{2}$ are positive-definite?
- **I.** ${x}^{T}\,Qx,$ where the eigenvalues of $Q$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$
- **II.** ${x}^{T}\,Rx,$ where the eigenvalues of $R$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=10$
- **III.** ${x}^{T}\,Sx,$ where the eigenvalues of $S$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8$

Select all that apply.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "III only."
correct answer is "III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Given a quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}Ax,$ we have the following theorem:

- $Q$ is positive-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are positive,

- $Q$ is positive semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-negative (note that positive semi-definite quadratic forms include all positive-definite quadratic forms),

- $Q$ is negative-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are negative,

- $Q$ is negative semi-definite if and only if all the eigenvalues of $A$ are non-positive (note that negative semi-definite quadratic forms include all negative-definite quadratic forms), and

- $Q$ is indefinite if and only if $A$ has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

With that in mind, let's examine our quadratic forms in turn.

- Quadratic form I is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $Q$ are positive (for example, ${\lambda }_{1}=0$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form II is *not* positive-definite since not all of the eigenvalues of $R$ are positive (${\lambda }_{1}=-6$ is not positive).

- Quadratic form III is positive-definite. Indeed, all of the eigenvalues of $S$ are positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given an equation of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).
$$

This is an autonomous equation because the right-hand side is a function of $y$ only. This means that, for a fixed value of $y,$ the slope does not vary with $x.$ 

Now, let's check each statement:

- Statement I is false. Consider a point of the form $(x,-2)$ where $x$ is arbitrary. We have

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(x,-2)}=-2+1=-1<0,
$$

and this implies that the slope at the point $(x,-2)$ is negative for any $x.$ Moreover, the slope at the point $(x,-2)$ is equal to $-1$ for any $x.$

- Statement II is true. Consider a point of the form $(x,-1)$ where $x$ is arbitrary. We have

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(x,-1)}=-1+1=0,
$$

and this implies that the slope at the point $(x,-1)$ is horizontal for any $x.$

- Statement III is false. Consider a point of the form $(x,1)$ where $x$ is arbitrary. We have

$$
{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{(x,1)}=1+1=2>0,
$$

and this implies that the slope at the point $(x,1)$ is positive for any $x.$ Moreover, the slope at the point $(x,1)$ is equal to $2$ for any $x.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

key_evidence.solution:
A connected region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/7d/7d6aea1a62fb290702630ef95ec86f4119e7c8fdd74b8148b62b66e5ac871b58.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

With that in mind, let's examine each of the regions:  

- Region I is simply connected. This is a connected region that does not contain holes.

- Region II is simply connected. This is a connected region that does not contain holes.

- Region III is simply connected. This is a connected region that does not contain holes.

- Region IV is not simply connected. Instead, this is a connected region that contains a hole.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III only."

A *generalized eigenvector* ${v}_{2}$ of rank $2$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda $ of a matrix $A$ is a nonzero vector such that

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-\lambda I\,}{\to }0,
$$

where ${v}_{1}\ne 0.$ Recall that an *eigenvector* is simply a generalized eigenvector of rank $1.$

With this in mind, let's examine our statements.

First, we compute $A-2I:$

$$
A-2I=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

- Next, we find the image of $v$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)v=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\ne 0
$$

- Since we got a nonzero vector in the last step, we now compute the image of $w$ under the action of $A-2I:$

$$
(A-2I)w=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0
$$

So, we obtain the following chain of maps:

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{v}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{w}\overset{A-2I\,}{\to }{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{0}
$$

Consider the function $f(x)$ whose graph is shown above.

$$
f(x)={\begin{aligned}x+\frac{1}{2},\, & 0<x<1, \\ 0,\, & \text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following statements are true?

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x$
- ${\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$
- $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function

Select all that apply.

key_evidence.solution:
For a function $f(x)$ to be a valid probability density function on a set $S,$ it must satisfy the following conditions:

- $f(x)\ge 0$ for all $x\in S$

- ${\int }_{S}f(x)\,\text{d}x=1$

Now, let's consider each statement in turn:

- Statement I is true. From the graph, we see that $f(x)$ is nonnegative for all $x.$

- Statement II is true. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}f(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{1}{2}]-[\frac{{0}^{2}}{2}+\frac{0}{2}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-0 \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Since statements I and II are true, $f(x)$ is a valid probability density function.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

- **I.** ${a}_{n}=-n{a}_{n-1}+4{a}_{n-2}$

key_evidence.worked_solution:
A recurrence relation is **linear (with constant coefficients)** if it expresses ${a}_{n}$ as a sum of previous terms ${a}_{n-1},…,{a}_{n-k}$ with constant coefficients, together with possibly a final term that depends only on $n:$

$$
{a}_{n}={s}_{1}{a}_{n-1}+{s}_{2}{a}_{n-2}+…+{s}_{k}{a}_{n-k}+g(n)
$$

where ${s}_{1},{s}_{2},…,{s}_{k}$ are constants and $g(n)$ is a function, often called a **forcing function**, that does not involve ${a}_{n}$ or its preceding terms. 

Let's examine each recurrence relation in turn.

- ${a}_{n}$ is not linear. The coefficient of the term $-n{a}_{n-1}$ is not constant.

- ${b}_{n}$ is linear. The term ${b}_{n-1}$ occurs only in the first power with constant coefficient.

- ${c}_{n}$ is not linear. The term ${c}_{n-1}^{2}$ is not in the first power.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

- ${c}_{n}$ is not homogeneous. The term $1$ of the expression doesn't contain preceding terms of the relation.

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Recall that a first-order linear system of differential equations with two dependent variables is a system of the form

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t)=a(t){x}_{1}(t)+b(t){x}_{2}(t)+f(t) \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t)=c(t){x}_{1}(t)+d(t){x}_{2}(t)+g(t).\end{aligned}
$$

If $f≡0$ and $g≡0$ (i.e., both $f$ and $g$ are zero functions), then the system is *homogeneous*. Otherwise, if at least one of $f$ or $g$ is not identically zero, the system is *inhomogeneous*.

With this in mind, let's inspect each system:

- System I is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=3, &  & b(t)=2, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-1, &  & d(t)=4, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

- System II is inhomogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $g≢0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=-1, &  & b(t)=1, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=-2, &  & d(t)=0, &  & g(t)=5\end{aligned}
$$

- System III is homogeneous since it can be written in the standard form with $f≡0$ and $g≡0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t)=0, &  & b(t)=0, &  & f(t)=0 \\ c(t)=7, &  & d(t)=3, &  & g(t)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only".

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{7}$ into ${R}^{7},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{7} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=7 \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$

Since $T$ is a linear transformation, we have that

$$
T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})\,⟹\,T({v}_{1}-{v}_{2})=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since ${v}_{1}-{v}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T)$ and ${v}_{1}\ne {v}_{2},$ we must have that $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement II is false. According to the invertible matrix theorem, since $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0},$ the transformation $T$ and the matrix $T$ are not invertible.

- Statement III is true. Since $T$ is not invertible, the invertible matrix theorem implies that $\text{nullity}(T)\ne 0.$ In turn, this means that $\text{nullity}(T)>0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Which of the following vector spaces are finite-dimensional?
- **I.** $D(R),$ the vector space of all differentiable functions on $R$
- **II.** ${R}^{100}$
- **III.** ${R}_{2000}[t],$ the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ of degree at most $2\,000$

questions.reason: Finite explicitly supplied independent cases; complete old-choice subsets; preserve database key.

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "II and III only."
correct answer is "II and III only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- $D(R)$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following subset of $D(R)$ is linearly independent:

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,{t}^{n}},\,n\in N.
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{t}^{i}=0
$$

for all $t\in R$ if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of $D(R)$  of size $n,$ which imples that $D(R)$ cannot have finite dimension.     .

- ${R}^{100}$ and ${R}_{2000}[t]$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({R}^{100})=100
$$

 
and

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{2000}[t])=2000+1=2\,001,
$$

are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
A *decoupled system* consists of equations depending on only one variable, such as

$$
{x}_{i}^{′}(t)={\lambda }_{i}{x}_{i}(t),
$$

where ${\lambda }_{i}$ is a constant. This means that we can solve each equation independently.  

In matrix form, a linear system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ is decoupled if $A$ is a diagonal matrix.

With this in mind, let's examine our systems.

- System II is decoupled since its corresponding matrix is diagonal.

- Systems I and III are *not* decoupled because their matrices are not diagonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

If $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto the line $y=-3x$ then, which of the following statements are true?

- $⟨1,3⟩$ belongs to the range of $T$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. 

- Statement I is false. 
Notice that the point $(1,3)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $y=-3x$ since $3\ne -3\cdot 1.$ Therefore, the vector $⟨1,3⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, 
since $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line passing through the origin, we have that the standard matrix $T$ is singular. Hence, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement III is false. 
For example,  the point $(1,-3)$ satisfies the equation  $y=-3x$ since $-3=-3\cdot 1.$ Therefore, the vector $⟨1,-3⟩\in \text{Im}(T).$ Thus, $\text{Im}(T)\ne {0}.$

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that when the image of a linear transformation $T$ in ${R}^{2}$ with the standard matrix $T$ is a one-dimensional line, then

$$
\text{rank}(T)=\text{rank}(T)=1
$$

and, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T) & =2-\text{rank}(T) \\  & =2-1 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn. 

- Statement I is false.
Notice that the point $(\frac{6}{5},1)$ does not satisfy the equation of the line $5y=6x$ since $5\cdot 1\ne \frac{6}{5}\cdot 6.$ Therefore, 
$⟨\frac{6}{5},1⟩\notin \text{Im}(T).$

- Statement II is true.
Since $T$ maps ${R}^{2}$ onto a line passing through the origin, we have that the standard matrix $T$ is singular. So, $\text{Ker}(T)\ne {0}.$

- Statement III is false.
Since  statement II is true we have that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim(Ker}(T))\ne 0.$

- **II.** If there exists a vector $v\notin \text{Im}(T),$ then $|T|\ne 0$

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Since $T$ is a linear transformation from ${R}^{n}$ into ${R}^{n},$ the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

 $T$ is a bijection (an invertible transformation) $\,⟺\,{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Im}(T)={R}^{n} \\  & \text{rank}(T)=n \\  & \text{Ker}(T)={0} \\  & \text{nullity}(T)=0\end{aligned}$ 

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, 

$$
\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Solving $x+y=0$ for $x,$ we get $x=-y.$ Therefore, any vector from $\text{Im}(T)$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-y \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]=y{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{1}}+z{{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{v}_{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that $\text{Ker}(T)=\text{Span}{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}.$ Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=2.$ Finally, according the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(T)+\text{nullity}(T) & =n \\ \text{rank}(T)+2 & =n.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. If $v\notin \text{Im}(T)$ then $\text{Im}(T)\ne {R}^{n}$, so, according to the invertible matrix theorem, $T$ is not a bijection. Thus, the matrix $T$ is not invertible, and, consequently, $|T|=0.$

- Statement III is false. Since $T({v}_{1})=T({v}_{2})=0$, then ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}\in \text{Ker}(T).$ But the vectors are linearly independent, therefore, the dimension of  $\text{Ker}(T)$ is at least $2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $Q$ is orthogonal if and only if

$$
Q{Q}^{T}={Q}^{T}Q=I.
$$

To check that a matrix is orthogonal, it is sufficient to check that the above equation is satisfied.

Moreover, we have the following properties:

- For any orthogonal matrix $Q,$ we have ${Q}^{-1}={Q}^{T}.$

- $(AB)^{T}={B}^{T}{A}^{T}$ for conformable matrices $A$ and $B.$

With that in mind, let's inspect each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. Computing the product $(2PQ)\cdot (2PQ)^{T},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(2PQ)\cdot (2PQ)^{T} & =2PQ\cdot 2{Q}^{T}{P}^{T} \\  & =4P(Q{Q}^{T}){P}^{T} \\  & =4P(I){P}^{T} \\  & =4I \\  & \ne I.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the following subtraction of two orthogonal matrices:

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The resulting matrix is not orthogonal since, for example, its first column is not normalized.

- Statement III is false. The inverse of an orthogonal matrix $P$ is given by ${P}^{-1}={P}^{T}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true".

key_evidence.worked_solution:
Let's examine our vector spaces.

- $D(R)$ is *not* finite-dimensional. To understand why, we first note that the following subset of $D(R)$ is linearly independent:

$$
{1,\,t,\,{t}^{2},\,…,{t}^{n}},\,n\in N.
$$

Indeed, we have that 

$$
{\sum }_{i=0}^{n}{x}_{i}{t}^{i}=0
$$

for all $t\in R$ if and only if ${x}_{i}=0$ for all $i=0,1,2,…,n.$ Therefore,  for any  $n\in N,$  there exists a linearly independent subset of $D(R)$  of size $n,$ which imples that $D(R)$ cannot have finite dimension.     .

- ${\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R)$ and ${R}_{200}[t]$ are finite-dimensional. Indeed, 

$$
\text{dim}({\text{M}}_{10\times 100}(R))=10\cdot 100=1\,000
$$

 
and

$$
\text{dim}({R}_{200}[t])=200+1=201,
$$

are both finite numbers.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

key_evidence.worked_solution:
The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, let's recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, ${a}_{11}=-2$ and

$$
det(A)=|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}|=-7.
$$

- Statement II is true. Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-2<0, \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3\end{aligned}|=-7<0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite.

- Statement III is true. Since the matrix $A$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a saddle point of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III."

The quadratic Taylor approximation of the function $f(x)$ about $x=a\in {R}^{3}$ is given by

$$
f(x)≈-7+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}A(x-a),
$$

where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** $det(A)>0$
- **II.** $A$ is positive-definite
- **III.** $a$ is a local maximum of $f$

Select all that apply. If none apply, leave all boxes unchecked.

key_evidence.worked_solution:
The point $a\in {R}^{n}$ is a critical point of the function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}.$ In such cases, we can classify $a$ as follows:

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is positive definite, then $a$ is a local minimum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is negative definite, then $a$ is a local maximum

- if ${f}^{″}(a)$ is neither positive-definite nor negative-definite, then $a$ is a saddle point

In this case, we have $A={f}^{″}(a).$ Now, before we examine the statements, we recall how to categorize quadratic forms.

Let ${Δ}_{i}$ for $i=1,2,…,n$  denote the leading principal minors of an $n\times n$ matrix $A.$ Then, according to Sylvester's criterion, the quadratic form ${x}^{T}\,A\,x$ (as well as the matrix $A$) is 

- positive-definite if and only if ${Δ}_{i}>0$ for all $i=1,2,…,n,$

- negative-definite if and only if, for all $i=1,2,…,n,$ we have ${Δ}_{i}<0$ when $i$ is odd, and ${Δ}_{i}>0$ when $i$ is even.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Indeed,

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 4 & -1 & -4\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5\cdot |\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ -1 & -4\end{aligned}|-2\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -4\end{aligned}|+4\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-5(11)-2(-4)+4(10) \\  & =-7<0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Δ}_{1} & ={a}_{11}=-5<0 \\ {Δ}_{2} & =|\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}|=11>0 \\ {Δ}_{3} & =|A|=-7<0\end{aligned}
$$

So, by Sylvester's criterion, the matrix $A$ is negative-definite.

- Statement III is true. Since the matrix $A$ is negative-definite, the critical point $a$ is a local maximum of $f.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

- **I.** ${y}^{″}+{y}^{′}-y={x}^{2},\,y(0)=1,\,y(2)=3$
- **II.** ${y}^{″}-4y=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2$
- **III.** ${y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+y={e}^{x}$

Select all that apply.

key_evidence.worked_solution:
If a second-order differential equation for the function $y(x)$ is given with two conditions specified at *different* locations in the domain of $y,$ then this is a **boundary value problem**.

Let's go through each equation in turn.

- The first system is a boundary value problem. It consists of a differential equation together with two conditions at different points in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=0$ and $x=2$).

- The second system is not a boundary value problem. The differential equation is together with two conditions at the *same* location in the domain of $y(x)$ (i.e., at $x=1$). This is an **initial value problem.**

- The third system is not a boundary value problem. It contains an equation only. No conditions are specified.

atomic_options.label: I
atomic_options.proof:
First, notice that all three differential equations are of the form

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=f(y).
$$

The phase line gives us the following information:

- The equilibrium solutions are $y=-3$ and $y=0.$

- $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-3,0)\cup (0,\infty ).$

- $f(y)$ is negative for $y\in (-\infty ,-3).$

With this in mind, let's study each of the given equations.

- We start by considering ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}(y+3).$

First, we see that $f(y)={y}^{2}(y+3),$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=-3,0.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

Now, we can construct a sign table for $f(y)$ as follows:

|  | $(-\infty ,-3)$ | $(-3,0)$ | $(0,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $y+3$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| ${y}^{2}$ | $+$ | $+$ | $+$ |
| $f(y)$ | $-$ | $+$ | $+$ |

So, we have that $f(y)$ is negative for  $y\in (-\infty ,-3),$ and $f(y)$ is positive for $y\in (-3,0)\cup (0,\infty ).$ This corresponds to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation I has the given phase line.

- Next, we consider ${y}^{′}=y(y+3)^{2}.$

First, $f(y)=y(y+3)^{2},$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=-3,0.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

However, we note that $f(y)<0$ for $y\in (-\infty ,-3)\cup (-3,0).$ This does *not* correspond to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation II does not have the given phase line.

- Finally, we consider ${y}^{′}={y}^{2}+3y.$

First, $f(y)=y(y+3),$ so $f(y)=0$ if $y=-3,0.$ So, the equilibrium solutions correspond to those shown in the phase line.

However, we note that $f(y)<0$ for $y\in (-3,0).$ This does *not* correspond to the arrows shown on the phase line.

Therefore, equation III does not have the given phase line.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Which of the following improper integrals are divergent?
- **I.** ${\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x$
- **II.** ${\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x$
- **III.** ${\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$

Select all that apply.

solution_confirmation: In conclusion, only integrals I and II are divergent.
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Let's work out each integral.

For the first integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{6}^{\infty }\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}\frac{1}{\sqrt{x-5}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[2\sqrt{x-5}]}_{6}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2\sqrt{6-5}) \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(2\sqrt{a-5}-2) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the second integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{3}\,{x}^{-2/3}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{x}^{1/3}]}_{1}^{a} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }(\sqrt[3]{a}-1) \\  & =\infty ,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral diverges.

For the third integral, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{-1}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{[-\frac{1}{x}]}_{a}^{-1} \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1+\frac{1}{a}) \\  & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

so the integral is convergent.

In conclusion, only integrals I and II are divergent.

- **I.** The quantity of fat, in grams per kilogram, in a sausage

key_evidence.worked_solution:
A random variable is a variable whose value is determined by the outcome of a trial or experiment. A *continuous* random variable is a random variable whose possible values are represented by an interval of real numbers.

Common examples of continuous random variables are shown in the diagram below.

![](images/05/05e3d893f6c069dce5b51dc7d9fa5830b44bca58fa071009548fde20ebe92c19.png)

With that in mind, let's consider each of the given statements.

- Statement I describes a continuous random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and its possible values correspond to the real interval $[0,1\,000].$

- Statement II does *not* describe a continuous random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, but its possible values are the integers $0,1,2,3,…,50,$ which do not correspond to an interval of real numbers.

- Statement III describes a  continuous random variable. Its value is determined by the result of an experiment, and its possible values correspond to the real interval $(0,\infty ).$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

- **U.** $U={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]}$
- **V.** $V={[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$
- **W.** $W={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]}$

solution_confirmation: correct answer is "U only"
correct answer is "U only
key_evidence.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
${{u}_{1},{u}_{2}},$
${{v}_{1},{v}_{2}},$ and 
${{w}_{1},{w}_{2}}$, respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{2}{5}-\frac{2}{5}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{5}+\frac{4}{5}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{5}+\frac{1}{5}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+1=1\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ only".

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=0.
$$

With that in mind, let's consider each vector field.

- Vector field I doesn't have a stream function. The partial derivatives are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=3+(-2y)\ne 0.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=1,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =2xy.\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=1+2xy\ne 0.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂x}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂y} & =-2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}=2x+(-2x)=0.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

- **II.** $Δx=\frac{0.6}{\lambda }$
